text:
In 2025, I moved into my new home right before Diwali.

No sofa, no bed, and we ate on the floor.  🤣 

But the walls had just been painted, and the whole place smelled like fresh paint.
That’s when it felt like a home. Before a single diya was lit, Diwali had already started.
I thought about that when I watched Asian Paints' new Diwali film, Tayaari Shuru, Tyohaar Shuru.

Most festive ads love the big night: the lamps, the sweets, the new clothes. This one starts earlier. It starts in the rush of getting ready.

That’s smart marketing. Every brand talks about Diwali night, so Asian Paints chose to talk about the weeks before it. It moves the focus from the festival to the preparations. Paint becomes the first step of the celebration, because it changes the room before anyone lights a lamp.

My new home taught me the same thing. Diwali doesn’t begin on the night itself. It begins with the preparations.

What’s the first thing you do to get your home ready for Diwali?

#AsianPaints #TayaariShuruTyohaarShuru

An influencer with 1.3 million followers died by suicide.

It’s truly a dark day for social media.

This has sparked a lot of conversations since he alleged cyberbullying as the reason of this drastic step.

Things worth always noting:

→ Suicide is never the solution. Life has many seasons, and God has a bigger plan for you 

→ Followers don’t equal happiness.

→ Criticism is not cyberbullying. Holding someone accountable is important, but it may be hard to find a line.

→ People love content, controversies and screenshots and often forget there’s a human behind it.

→ Virality has consequences. Sometimes negative ones too.

→You can disagree with someone’s actions without trying to destroy their life.


We talk so much about reach, engagement and building a personal brand.

Harish’s death is a heartbreaking reminder that there is a real person behind every profile.

My condolences to his family and loved ones.

text:
24.07 billion transactions in a month. 

What does that number really tell us?

It tells us that digital payments have become a part of everyday economic activity.

With affordable mobile internet becoming widely accessible after Jio's entry into the market, digital payment platforms like UPI became easier for millions of people to use in their daily lives.

✅A tea seller receives a payment.
✅ A freelancer collects a fee.
✅ A family transfers money.
✅ A small retailer pays a supplier.

Individually, these transactions look ordinary.
Collectively, they reveal a significant change in how money moves through the economy.

For finance professionals, UPI offers several interesting areas to study:

• The reduction in friction during small-value transactions.
• The changing payment preferences of consumers.
• The potential for better transaction records.
• The opportunities and challenges of serving small businesses digitally.

However, transaction volume alone does not measure economic progress. ❌

We must also consider transaction value, active users, merchant adoption, failed transactions, fraud and the quality of access.

A high transaction count is an important indicator of digital adoption, but it is not a complete measure of financial inclusion.

The real question is not just how many payments India makes digitally.

It is how effectively digital payments help people participate in the formal economy.

text:
I say this to founders all the time.

Your brand positioning should leave room for the business you want to build next.

Because when you're building a business, it's easy to focus on what you've achieved so far. But your brand also needs to communicate where you're headed.

That's what caught my attention about Hygienic Research Institute (HRIPL)  refreshed corporate identity and tagline, “Where Beauty Evolves.”

HRI operates across hair colour, hair care, skincare and professional salon solutions, with brands like Vasmol, Florozone, Streax and Streax Professional.

That's a diverse portfolio. And the opportunity ahead is to keep building on it as consumer preferences and aspirations evolve.

What I like about “Where Beauty Evolves” is that it leaves room for what's next.

New ideas. Changing consumer needs. Continued innovation backed by scientific expertise.

HRI's refreshed identity sets out its ambition for the future of beauty and personal care. The interesting part will be how that vision takes shape across its brands and the solutions it develops for consumers.

A question for founders: does your current positioning reflect the business you're building towards, or only the one you have today?

#BrandPositioning #FounderMarketing #BrandStrategy

Dheeraj Arora 
Priyancka Puri  Saloni Sharma

text:
My highest paying client paid me $7,500 for a month.
My least paying client paid me $300.

The gap between them taught me more than any course or mentor.

1. The $300 client had the most opinions.

Eleven rounds of edits on one post. 
Voice notes at 11pm. 
“Can we make it pop?” (Nobody has ever defined “pop.”)

They also fired me in 2 months.

The $7,500 client showed up once a week on calls. We worked together for 1.2 years.

2. Price is a filter, not just a number.

At $7,500, clients arrive with a goal, a decision-maker and an approved budget.
At $300, you are a quick experiment.

3. But a $300 client can be equally important.

While there are cons, they did:

- give me my first international testimonial which I needed
- let me try my hand at new things for them
- made me confident of getting results

A cheap client can be a stepping stone. 

Just don’t build your house on one.

What I do now:

→ Scope in writing before any work starts
→ Two rounds of edits, included
→ Anything extra → priced extra

Question:

What’s the lowest you’ve ever charged, and what did it actually do for you?

comments.text:
Saheli, consulting has one of the most fascinating economic contradictions.
Sometimes the client paying the least expects the consultant to be available 24 hours a day, seven days a week, including public holidays, family celebrations and possibly during a medical emergency!
Meanwhile, the client paying substantially more often understands the value of expertise, respects agreed boundaries and actually allows the professional to do the work.
 I have learned that the most expensive client is not necessarily the one with the smallest invoice.
It is the one who purchases a bicycle and expects a chauffeur-driven Rolls-Royce, complete with unlimited fuel and lifetime maintenance!
But your observation about smaller clients is equally important.
Some provide invaluable learning, testimonials, referrals and opportunities to establish credibility.
The distinction is whether we are making a deliberate investment in the relationship or unknowingly financing the client's expectations.
A low fee can be a strategic decision. Unlimited expectations at that fee are a commercial disaster.
And perhaps the most important lesson?
A discount on professional fees should never automatically become a discount on professional respect!

Autumn in Almaty is a strange beauty.

I’m leaving with a camera roll full of mountains, cafe pictures, little discoveries, and reminders of why I love travelling. 🇰🇿

A few things I genuinely loved about Almaty:

~ The mountains. I dont think you can ever get used to seeing snow-capped peaks in the background of an ordinary city day.
~ The cafe culture and the people. Slighlty reserved but they try to be as friendly, consider the language barrier.
~ Trying flavours I dont usually get back home in India

 Its a good reminder of how much of the world exists outside your little bubble.

As someone who spends a LOT of time creating content, building businesses, and thinking about what to do next, travelling forces me to do something I often forget: Be present. 


Almaty, you were a lovely surprise. ❤️

text:
For a marketer, a label is not just a compliance requirement. It is the first message a brand delivers on the shelf. So what happens when that message is the same for every product? 

 
That is a question worth asking as India shapes its approach to Front-of-Pack Labelling. 

Reformulating a product is a significant investment in R&D, sourcing, testing, packaging and consumer re-education. Brands make that investment when it helps them stand apart. But if a reformulated product carries the same “high” warning as one that has made no changes, what is the incentive for a manufacturer to invest? 

This is where the threshold, and the methodology behind it, deserve a closer look. Where the line is drawn, and whether a single “high” signal is the only way of expressing it, will decide which products get flagged and how consumers read them. A signal that only says a threshold has been crossed cannot show how far, or how much progress has been made towards it. 

 

That could discourage the very reformulation FOPL hopes to encourage. And for consumers, it could mean fewer better options on the shelf. 

 
How much has the threshold been exceeded? How does one product compare with another? What does the number mean for the portion actually being consumed? 

These questions matter because food choices rarely happen in isolation. Serving size, frequency of consumption and the broader diet all shape what a nutrient level means. Similar products can have different nutritional profiles even when they carry the same warning. 

 
This is where a little personalisation goes a long way: helping consumers see what a product means for their portion, their diet and their household. 

That requires clear communication on the pack, access to meaningful nutritional information, and sustained efforts to build nutrition literacy. 

Because the best consumer choice is an informed one. Empowering consumers is not about telling them what to choose. It is about giving them the tools to understand their choices better. 

Perhaps that is the opportunity for FOPL: not simply to create a more visible label, but a more informed decision-making process, one that also rewards the brands doing the work to improve. 

#ConsumerChoice #FOPL #NutritionLiteracy #FoodLabelling #ConsumerAwareness #Reformulation #FoodIndustry

text:
Every week I spend 15 hours researching trending formats, viral topics, and content ideas for my socials.

I decided to use AI to scrape trending topics, but that’s actually the wrong approach.

Your AI Agents need to know which trends actually fit your three content pillars. For example, mine are:
- Marketing & Strategy
- Online Business Tools
- Practical AI Usecases
This is basically what HubSpot Context Home is built to fix.

Agents perform better when they understand how a business actually works:

~ it’s target demographics
~ customer segments,
~ audience painpoints

Context Home is where that information lives and gets maintained, so every agent running on HubSpot has what it needs to act without constant supervision.

It can understand which formats have worked for your audience before, and which ones flopped even though they were "viral." What counts as on-brand for me versus what's just noise I'd never post.

I am still the boss, and I take care of what is finally put for production but this process easily saves me two working days a month.

Last month, I had multiple business expenses.  🫠 

~ Flights 
~ Uber Rides 
~ Travel Bookings

That’s a sign business is going well. That’s also a sign that finances will be a mess to manage!  🥲 

So when I heard Deel automated this at 10,000+ receipts a month, across 150 countries, each with different rules for what even counts as a valid expense, I wanted to know how.

Here’s how they did it, 100% remotely:

- Their finance lead ran through one expense start to finish on her screen
- An agent built on Akai watched that single session.
- It copied both the process and the logic behind it.

Simple but crucial things like:

- the country has to be checked first
- multiple receipts needs to be split and reviewed line by line.
- Just working them out from watching her do the job once.

Deel has reportedly added $140M ARR without hiring more people. Want to try it out?

text:
“Content Creators are getting richer than engineers!” headlines say.

“These girls dancing on reels make more money than me,” I hear often.

I work in the Creator Economy, and a very common problem is dismissing influencer work as “not real work.”

But wait, did you know it’s a $250B industry?

And even on a micro level, it involves:

→ Scriptwriting
→ Filming
→ Editing
→ Advertising
→ Modelling
→ Negotiating with major brands
→ Financial management
→ Team management
→ Community management

And then there’s the part that’s hardest to quantify:

Influence.

You may know how to analyse a supply chain.

You may know how to reduce costs.

You may know how to run a business.

But that doesn’t automatically mean you know how to build an audience, earn its trust, or move people to action.

And that’s the point:

A skill doesn’t become less valuable because it’s associated with, creators, beauty, fashion, or social media.

Work doesn’t have to look like your work to be real work.

If it was that easy, everyone would be successful doing it.

text:
SUPER Weird interests I have that made me a better marketeer

1. My Reading Taste. 😄 

I read a range of works, such as:

Foucault → to understand power, discourse & surveillance
Sherlock Holmes → observation & inference
Dostoevsky → contradiction & psychology

Because the best insights rarely come from marketing books.


2. Solving Puzzles 🤔 

I spend an embarrassing amount of time solving puzzles on

- Murdle Website
- The New York Times Games and 
- Puzzling Stack Exchange.

It trains me to spot patterns, connect seemingly unrelated clues and question my first assumption.

3. Watching movies 😊 

I don't just watch movies for entertainment anymore.
I notice how characters are introduced, what makes a scene memorable, how brands are positioned, what visual codes signal status, and why certain stories stay with us.

- Parasite teaches you about class.
- The Social Network teaches you about ambition.
- Barbie teaches you about cultural conversation.
- Mad Men teaches you about persuasion.

Every good movie is basically a masterclass in human attention + storytelling + culture.

What's one strange interest that indirectly helped you at work? 🤫

document.title: How To Use AI for Visuals

text:
AI has officially made boring visuals unnecessary. 

As a marketer, I’m taking full advantage of it. 😌

Here are 5 ways I’m using AI for visuals right now:

1. Creative concepts

Have a random idea from Pinterest?
I can actually bring it to life.
For example, I created a fun “mini-me” visual for a dessert brand.

My workflow:
→ Pinterest for inspiration
→ ChatGPT for prompting
→ Runway for execution + animation

2. Turning screenshots into stories

Instead of posting a boring screenshot of something I found online…

- I turn it into a visual> Add myself.
- Create a setting.
- Give the screenshot context.
More fun right?

3. Brand identity exploration

Starting a new brand?

AI can help you quickly explore:
→ Logo directions
→ Colour palettes
→ Typography
→ Packaging ideas
→ Brand personality

You don't need to blindly start designing from scratch.
Use AI to explore what you like first.

(You’ll still want a good designer like Devanshi Saraogi to take it from concept to a proper brand system.)

4. Photoshoot concepts

Found a cool photoshoot idea?
You don't always need to book a studio immediately.
I used Runway's Agent to bring a birthday photoshoot concept to life.

5. Rich product visuals

This is probably one of my favourites.
AI can create incredibly detailed product imagery like this chocolate visual where you can almost feel the velvetiness.
And the best part?
Those images can then be turned into videos.

And for marketers, that's HUGE.

Save this for the next time you have a visual idea but no budget, photographer, studio or designer on standby. 👀

Which of these would you try first?

text:
Why Are Asian Cultures Obsessed With Cats?

I was in Vietnam for a month, and realised cat cafes are quite common here. At Oleoleobooks, I met 8 cats at once.


Now I understand there are:
- countries in which the cat is beloved,
- countries in which the dog is beloved,
- countries in which neither animal is particularly welcome in the house.

Still, you notice a pattern. 

Cats are a recurring motif in Japanese Literature.
In China, cats have a long history as domestic and symbolic animals.
Cat cafes are also popular in several asian countries.


The familiar Western explanation is that cats are cute.
But cats are cute almost everywhere. What differs is what a culture does with that fact.

Here's my two cents:

A cat is a visual language.
A cat sticker sent instead of a sentence.
A cat face, with its fluffy cuteness is a sense of comfort.

And reflective of modern society, cats are extraordinarily good at living between worlds. 

- Inside and outside.
- Wild and domestic.
- Independent and dependent.

Well what do you think? Why are Asian countries obsessed with cats?

I am excited to attend more events soon.

Will community become the next competitive advantage for brands?

text:
If you’re not being creative in 2026, you’re irrelevant.

AI tools like Gemini, Higgsfield and Converge have made it easier than ever.

Want my ideas? You got it.

1. Put your product into an impossible scenario.

> Meet Cleopatra and ask her beauty secrets.
> Put your skincare product in an ancient Egyptian beauty ritual.
> Hermione used the wrong potion, but your product saves the day!

2. Bring historical figures into your campaign.

> Ask Einstein to explain your product.
> Let Shakespeare write your ad.
> Imagine Steve Jobs reviewing your startup.

3. Turn your product into a character.

> Make your coffee brand a dramatic morning person.
> Or your makeup brand a DIVA. 
> Let your product complain about its competitors.

4. Create moments that would be impossible to film.

> Your product falling from the sky into a city.
> A giant version of your product walking through  New York.

5. Make the audience curious.

> Don’t show the product immediately.
> Build a story around the question: “What is going on?”

You don’t need a Hollywood budget to test them.

♻️ Repost so more marketers start thinking beyond boring ads.

text:
At 15, a teacher told me I will be a "broke writer."
At 25, I had made multiple six figures, built on writing.

Here's everything that worked out for me.

Year 1: A random guy paid me to write reviews. I did. Made $1 Per review. Shocking right?
Year 2: Wrote more reviews. Charged lesser, called it bulk pricing. Started posting YT Videos. Made no money.
Year 3: Made $300 a month. All through writing. Still posting on YT. No money.
Year 4: Started learning marketing. Storytel started sponsoring me, at $1000-$2000 per month on Youtube. 
Year 5: Got $500 paying international recurring clients. $1000 paying one-off sponsors.
Year 6: Got multiple $2000 per month clients. Started a Freelance Program. Worked with Global Sponsors. 
Year 7: Got my first few $5000 per month projects. Steep learning curve. Stopped working with sponsors.
Year 8: Took a pause. Got married. By the time I came back, everything was AI.
Year 9: Started Travelling. Working with better clients, students and resumed working with top brands.

Year 10 is now :) I hope you're having a good time following my journey.

It wasn't a straight line. There were years I made almost nothing.
There were years I thought I was doing everything wrong.

But every year, I added another skill:
Writing → marketing → content → sales → business.

10 years later, I'm still writing.
Just not for $1 a review.

10 design skills that everyone needs to learn 

Master two of these and you'll be ahead of 99% of people. 

Made with Devanshi Saraogi <3

Save this, you'll want it later.

1. Brand Strategy

Learn how to build brands that are distinct, memorable, and strategically positioned.
Resources:
• The Brand Gap by Marty Neumeier
• Zag by Marty Neumeier
• The Brand Flip by Marty Neumeier

2. Visual Hierarchy

Learn how to guide the eye to what matters first, next, and last.
Resources:
• Satori Graphics on YouTube
• Laws of UX
• Grid Systems in Graphic Design by Josef Müller-Brockmann

3. Design Basics

If you're a non-designer, this is where you start. Master composition, colour, spacing, and layout.

Resources:
• CalArts Graphic Design Specialization on Coursera
• Canva Design School
• Satori Graphics on YouTube

4. Typography

Font pairing and type hierarchy are what separate “homemade” from “premium.”
Resources:
• Typewolf
• Practical Typography by Matthew Butterick
• Fonts In Use

5. Brand Identity

Turn strategy into a visual system people can instantly recognise.
Resources:
• Branding in Five and a Half Steps
• Brand New by UnderConsideration
• Logo Geek

6. Creative Direction

Learn to turn strategy into taste, make creative decisions, and defend your vision.
Resources:
• Basic Arts on YouTube
• Eye on Design by AIGA
• The Futur on YouTube

7. Motion Design

Static design is quiet. Motion makes people stop. Basic motion skills can instantly modernise your work.
Resources:
• Ben Marriott on YouTube
• Jake in Motion on YouTube
• Motionographer

8. Presentations

Great design means little if you can't present it, price it, and defend it to a client.
Resources:
• The Futur on YouTube
• Slide:ology by Nancy Duarte
• Duarte

9. Packaging Design

Packaging is brand strategy you can hold. Learn how to communicate a brand in seconds.
Resources:
• The Dieline
• Packaging of the World
• Behance Packaging Design

10. Creative Workflows + AI

Learn which AI tools actually save time and which ones are just hype.
Resources:
• Futurepedia
• Matt Wolfe on YouTube
• The Rundown AI
You don't need all 10.
You need two, done properly.
Save this for when you're ready to pick. ♻️

text:
By 25, I owned a home and a car. 

On paper, I am successful. But I think it's deeper than that.

Here are 5 Things that actually make me feel Rich.

1. I protect my mornings like they're sacred. 

- A warm glass of water. 
- Breakfast, milk coffee(no black coffee you don't tempt me!).
- No phone, no noise, no one else's agenda. 

Just me, waking up on my own terms before the world asks anything of me.

2. I reduce my outflow. 

I just talk to two people daily, my husband and my business lead. Everyone else gets less of me, and I'm at peace with that. Energy is currency. I stopped spending it on relationships that don't ask for depth.

3. I never let my brain go still. 

One week I'm learning Russian.
The next, I'm reading about how the detective genre took shape in the 1700s. The week after, I'm deep in the newest AI tools.

None of it "adds up" on paper, but makes me a great conversationalist.

4. I don't buy things. I buy time and health. Good food. Good books. 

That's it, that's the list. I save 80% of my income toward one goal: a house by the beach, where I'll start my family on my own terms.

5. I create impact, in ways that come naturally to me. 

Through my opinions, my choices, and simply the way I live....visibly, unapologetically. If it moves even one person closer to her own version of wealth, it was worth saying out loud.

None of this is about the money. It's about becoming someone money finds hard to leave.

If this resonated, save it.

text:
Want to get rich faster? Understand there’s 4 types of leverage.


There are only so many hours in a day, so if your growth depends entirely on your effort, eventually you hit a ceiling.

Leverage is what allows the same effort to produce a much bigger result.

There are 4 types of leverage worth building:

1. Knowledge leverage- you basically know what others don’t

Your knowledge becomes leverage when it helps you make better decisions, solve problems faster, or avoid expensive mistakes.

✅Best for:

People early in their careers, founders, specialists, and anyone entering a new field.

Learn deeply. Then turn what you know into frameworks, systems, content, or decisions that can be reused.

Being from a simple middle class family, this is what I focused on early on. 

2. Network leverage- who knows you and who you know

A strong network gives you access to opportunities that effort alone cannot create.

The right introduction can save months.
The right relationship can open a door you couldn’t open yourself.

✅Best for:

Entrepreneurs, salespeople, leaders, recruiters, investors, and anyone whose success depends on opportunities and collaboration.

This is what I did in the first few years of my career.

3. Skill leverage: become unusually good at something valuable

A valuable skill compounds.

The better you become, the more valuable your time becomes… and the more opportunities you attract.

✅ Best for:
Anyone who wants to increase their earning power or become difficult to replace.

Don’t try to master everything.

Find one skill that is valuable, rare, and aligned with where you want to go.


My answer? Content.

4. Time leverage - make your time work beyond the hours you spend

This is where growth really starts to scale.

Systems, automation, delegation, technology, and assets allow work to keep producing results without requiring your constant attention.

Best for:
Founders, managers, creators, and anyone who has already built enough expertise to know what should need them and shouldn’t.

Which is the unfair leverage you are building on? Tell me in a comment.

text:
10 Underrated Ways to Go Viral in 2026 

1. Comment on breaking news within 30 minutes
   ↳ AI company launches a new model → "3 things this means for freelancers."

2.  Turn viral comments into content
   ↳ Instead of creating from scratch, find a top-performing comment under a viral post and expand it into, a carousel, short video or post.

3. Predict trends before they happen
   ↳ Even if you're only partly right, predictions spark discussion.

4. Respond to industry controversies
   ↳ Instead of taking an extreme position, explain why you agree or disagree with evidence.

5.  Share "live experiments"
   ↳ "Trying to get 1,000 newsletter subscribers in 30 days." - People love efforts.

6. Analyze why something went viral
   ↳ Instead of sharing the viral content itself, explain it. Viral fuels viral.

7. Be the first to review new features/products/content in your niche.
   ↳ Movie niche? Review Odysseus. Tech niche? Review Pixel 11 Pro. Early reviews often rank well and get shared.

8. Create "before everyone else" guides
   ↳ "How marketers should prepare for the next Instagram update." - Being early often matters more than being comprehensive.

9. Build on someone else's viral idea - Trend riding.
   ↳ Take a popular post from your niche or generic, and add a missing perspective.

10. Publish "insider observations"
   ↳ Share patterns you've noticed before they're widely discussed. Examples:
"After auditing 100 LinkedIn profiles, everyone makes these three mistakes."

♻️ Repost to actually try these out.

text:
I walked into KEEMTI expecting to browse a few jewellery designs.

I walked out genuinely impressed by how differently they're building the brand.
The first thing that stood out? The designs. Elegant, wearable, and thoughtfully crafted. Not just for weddings or special occasions, but for everyday moments. The kind of jewellery you can wear to work, brunch, or a dinner date without it feeling over the top.

As I spoke to the team, I learned what makes Keemti different.
Founded by Armaan Kothari, a third-generation jeweller with over a decade of experience in the diamond and jewellery industry, Keemti is built on a simple belief: diamonds shouldn't be reserved only for life's biggest milestones.

Coming from a family with over 45 years of expertise in the jewellery business, Armaan has created a brand that combines generations of craftsmanship with a modern, transparent way of buying jewellery.

Their pricing strategy is what struck me the most. By eliminating middlemen across the supply chain, they've made diamond jewellery far more accessible without compromising on quality. Their certified lab grown diamonds start at around ₹30,000 per carat, a price point that's incredibly difficult to match in the market, while maintaining exceptional craftsmanship, transparency, and value.

What really stood out to me is that this vision has also earned the confidence of Nikhil Kamath, who has backed Keemti as an investor and is actively involved in an advisory and operational capacity. When someone known for identifying disruptive consumer businesses chooses to back a brand, it says a lot about the opportunity they're building. Alongside Kavin Shah as an investor and Mr. Sunil Kothari as Chairman, Keemti is bringing together deep industry expertise with a modern approach to building a consumer-first jewellery brand.

Today, Keemti has stores across Pune, Mumbai, Indore, and Delhi, along with a strong e-commerce presence, and they're expanding rapidly with plans to reach 30+ stores by September.

It's exciting to see a homegrown brand challenging conventions and making fine diamond jewellery more accessible for a new generation of consumers.
If you haven't explored Keemti yet, it's definitely a brand worth discovering.

Visit https://keemtijewels.com/ to check it out yourself.

Show the mistake before showing the success.
Make the audience choose between two options instead of asking an open-ended question.
Leave one useful detail exclusively in the comments.
Build content around questions customers repeatedly ask in sales calls.
Say less. Curiosity gaps outperform information dumps when used well.
But there’s an important distinction:
Good marketing engineers curiosity. Bad marketing manufactures deception.
The best tactics get the click and make people glad they clicked.

text:
I spent 25 mornings in Mauritius. 🏖️ 🇲🇺 

By day 3, I stopped reaching for my phone.
By day 10, I stopped counting the days.
By day 25, I was a completely changed person.

Every sunrise and sunset on the beach, with me as their witness.

I run a media company from wherever I want.
Yet, most of my "free" mornings back home look nothing like this. 

I am usually glued to my phone, disconnected from nature.

Three things I'm taking home to India:

1. The phone waits.
 
Coffee first, silence first. Nothing in my inbox needs me so urgently.

2. Boredom is not the enemy.

It's okay to just sit. Not do anything at all.

3. Freedom I don't use isn't freedom.
I built a business that lets me work from anywhere. 
But...For years, I forgot to actually be anywhere.

25 mornings taught me more about pacing my life than $250K can.

What would your mornings look like if no one, including you, was rushing them?
That's the version I'm building toward now.

text:
I fired my entire marketing team 🙂‍↕️  and replaced them with AI.

except....I actually didn't. 

Every week, I see posts saying:
"AI replaced my team."

Darling, it shows. 🙂‍↕️ 

Here are the roles I'm still happily paying for:


1. Script Writer

Sure, AI can spit out 15 hooks with 25 body variations. But a scriptwriter with 5 years of experience knows why people actually stick. 

2. Video Editor 

I have multiple video editors, and each of them are irreplaceable because their taste and aesthetic sense is different. You can't buy taste, you build it.


3. Client Strategist

This is the most important person for my business. They strategise my content, my client content and even help coach my marketing students. 

It's also the highest-paid role on my team

4. Graphic Designer

Ipsit Saha deserves a shout out here, for years he has been behind my personal and client content, and I am so proud of his work now at WebVeda.com

5. Brand Manager

This person makes me more money every month! They handle outreach and ensuring my name is in the right rooms, and at the right time so I get good brand opportunities.

Sure we use AI to 

- make our processes faster
- edit faster, ideate better, create more
- create images, videos, and creative concepts

But trying to replace the entire marketing team? That's a dying move.

Repost this if you're tired of the "AI replaced my whole team" posts. ♻️

Which role do you think becomes more valuable because of AI?

text:
Every year, I read at least 50 books.

I don’t spend my entire day reading.

I simply make reading non-negotiable.

Here’s the math:

📖 Average book: 250 pages

50 books = 12,500 pages a year

That sounds like a lot…

Until you divide it.

➡️ 12,500 pages ÷ 365 days = 34 pages a day

That’s roughly 25–30 minutes of reading.

Or:

• 15 minutes with your morning coffee (15 pages)
• 15 minutes before bed (20 pages)

That’s it.

If 30 minutes feels too much, start smaller.

✅ Read 10 pages a day.
That’s 3,650 pages a year.

At an average of 250 pages per book, you’ll finish 14–15 books.

I also read a lot of Audiobooks and Graphic Novels 🧘‍♀️


And it is a huge priority for me to actually enjoy my work and life :)

What’s one book that changed the way you think? Drop your recommendation below. 👇

text:
School taught you to memorize.
Nobody taught you to actually get smarter.

These 5 habits will change that:

→ Learn languages with poetry

- I have picked up more than 200 words in 5 languages I don't speak,
- Read poems, song lyrics, quotes in another language.
- You also  pick up nuance, cultural context, and precision, hings Duolingo can't teach.

→ Capitals of countries

 Don't stop at the capital. Add one landmark. One historical fact. One population stat. You'll retain 10x more because now it means something.

→ Sketch things you don't understand

If you can't draw it, you probably don't understand it.
Try: engines, business models, AI systems.

→ Reverse-engineer everyday objects

Pick one item every week. A pen. An umbrella. A coffee machine.
Ask: why is it designed this way? What problem does it solve?

→ Keep a commonplace book
 
Collect quotes, ideas, observations, questions.
Da Vinci did it. John Locke did it.
It's a centuries-old habit that still works.

Save this for when you need a hobby that actually builds you.

text:
At 17, I was happy making ₹10,000 a month.

By 21, I had 20x’d that income.


If you’re in your 20s and want to win faster, here’s the simple guide I’d give you:

1. Learn skills people pay for

Not “interesting” skills.
Not “maybe useful one day” skills.

I mean skills that solve real business problems:
• writing
• sales
• marketing
• design
• operations
• AI / automation
• communication

If a skill can make someone money, save them time, or reduce their stress it can make you money too.

2. Your income grows when your usefulness grows

Want to earn more?

Ask better questions:

• What problem do I solve?
• Who is willing to pay for it?
• How can I solve it better than most people my age?

The market rewards value, not potential.

3. Don’t just consume. Build

Read, yes.
Learn, yes.
Take courses, yes.

But also:
• write online
• make projects
• freelance
• document what you’re learning
• sell something small
• build proof of work

Consumption makes you informed.
Creation makes you visible.

4. Get in rooms that stretch you

Your life can change with:
• one mentor
• one client
• one opportunity
• one room where people think bigger than you do

If everyone around you has the same fears, same habits, and same excuses, your growth will slow down without you even noticing.

5. Don’t increase your lifestyle as fast as your income

One of the best things I did in my early years:
I didn’t try to look rich.

I tried to become financially stable.

Use the extra money to:
• buy time
• invest in learning
• build a safety net
• start something of your own

Flexing is expensive.
Freedom is a better purchase.

Your 20s can change your entire life.

But only if you stop treating them like a waiting room.

What’s one thing your 20s have taught you so far?

text:
At 18
→  I charged $100/month for complete social media management.

At 23
→   I charged $100/hour just for people to pick my brain.

Same internet. Very different business.
The difference wasn’t “more hustle.”

At 18, my offer looked like this:
- content creation
- captions
- posting
- strategy
- “can you also just quickly…” work

All for $100/month.

At 23, people paid me $100 for one hour because they didn’t just want a social media manager.

They wanted:

- clarity on branding
- strategy for  long term growth
- audience insight for real monetisation!


That shift happened when I stopped selling tasks and started selling thinking.

If you’re undercharging right now, here’s how I’d fix it:

1) Stop saying “I do social media management”

That tells me what you do.
Not why you’re worth paying for.

2) Productize your offer

Don’t sell:
“I’ll do whatever you need on social media.”

Sell what you swear works :

- 12 content pieces/month
- monthly content calendar
- lead-gen CTA strategy
- repurposing across 2 platforms


3) Separate execution from strategy

If you’re doing both, price them separately.

This is how you stop being paid like an assistant for work that actually requires a brain.

4) Build proof around outcomes, not effort

Don’t say:
“I worked 5 hours on this”
“I made 30 posts”
“I managed everything”

Say:
“This messaging shift increased leads by 450%.”
“This positioning made got us 31 new clients from our ICP.”

Clients don’t buy your "effort". They buy the result.

5) Start charging for access to your brain

This is the part freelancers ignore for way too long.
You do not need to wait until you’re “famous” to sell strategy calls.

If people already ask you:
“What should I post?”
“Can you review my page?”
“How do I price this?”
…you already have the seed of a consulting offer.

Start with:

45–60 min audit calls
content strategy intensives
launch planning calls

Free resources I’d use if I were rebuilding this from scratch

→  Alex Hormozi’s offer/value content on YouTube
→  Justin Welsh’s content strategy content
→  HubSpot Blog guides on content marketing, social media strategy, buyer journeys.
→  Google Trends to understand what your niche is actively searching for.
→  Use Meta Ad Library to study how brands position products and offers.
Read newsletters/blogs from creators who teach audience building, not just aesthetics.

text:
In 1987, two brothers from Kanpur launched a detergent brand.

- No multinational backing.

- No premium shelf placement.

- No massive advertising budgets.

But they had a belief. Indian consumers deserved quality products at an accessible price point.

That brand went on to become one of India's most recognized household names: Ghadi.

But how did Ghadi make it in an already competitive market?

By focusing on the Aam Aadmi.

→ Cheaper prices.

→ Deeper distribution.

→ Tier-2 and Tier-3 towns first.

It worked.

Today, Ghadi holds 20% of India's detergent market and generates a whopping ₹5,000 crore in annual revenue.

The second-largest detergent brand in the country.

But Murli Dhar Gyanchandani didn't stop at detergent.

In 1995, his family launched Red Chief, turning Kanpur's leather industry into a national premium brand with 3,200+ outlets across 16 states.

Then came Namaste India, Pro Ease sanitary pads, and Venus soap.

His net worth: ₹11,000 crore+.

Most people miss something about this story.

He didn't disrupt a market by being louder than the competition.

He won by seeing who everyone else ignored, and serving them well.

Consistently.

For decades.

The biggest fortunes in India weren't built by chasing premium.

They were built by respecting the mass market enough to actually show up for it.

Which Indian business origin story surprised you most?

Drop it in the comments. I'll feature the best ones. 👇

text:
For a month, I watched my sister obsess over the Diet Coke shortage in India.
Every grocery run ended the same way:

"Did they have Diet Coke?"No.
"Check that store." No.
"Blinkit?" No.

At some point, I was annoyed:
Why can't she just... drink something else?
There are hundreds of beverages on the shelf.
- Regular Coke.
- Coke Zero.
- Pepsi.
- God sake...Sparkling water.

Surely they're all close enough? Apparently not.

In India, Diet Coke is marketed primarily as an identity.

It's associated with:

> Urban professionals
> Fitness-conscious consumers
> Creatives, founders, marketers, and young professionals
> Premium cafes and restaurants
> "Low-calorie lifestyle" signaling

The product is essentially selling:
"I care about health, but I still enjoy cola."

During the shortage, "Diet Coke parties" emerged in cities like Delhi and Mumbai. 

What's remarkable is that Diet Coke has developed a community that takes decades to build.

People:
- Post aesthetic Diet Coke photos
- Carry cans to work, feature it in desk setup
- Joke about addiction

But that's just me. Why do you think Indians are obsessed with Diet Coke?

text:
Sundays hit different when you are Bengali. 😗 

For many Bengalis, Sunday isn't just a day of the week

Sunday is aaraam (comfort), nostalgia, food, stories, and unhurried conversations.

1. Sunday Morning = Late Wake-Up + Newspaper Ritual

A classic Bengali Sunday often begins differently from weekdays:
No rush for office or school.
A cup of cha (tea).
A thick newspaper spread across the table.
Discussions about politics, cricket, cinema, literature, and neighborhood gossip.

2. For an entire generation, Sunday means the iconic radio program:
Sunday Suspense on Mirchi
People would:
> Wait all week for the next episode.
> Listen with lights dimmed.
> Discuss twists afterward.

Stories by writers like:

- Satyajit Ray
- Shirshendu Mukhopadhyay
- Samaresh Majumdar
- Adrish Bardhan
became part of countless Sunday afternoons.

Even today, many Bengalis associate Sunday with mystery, ghosts, thrillers, and headphones.

3. Adda: The Sacred Bengali Activity
There is perhaps no cultural practice more Bengali than adda.

Adda means:
> Conversation without agenda.
> Philosophy without deadlines.
> Politics without solutions.
> Literature without exams.
A Sunday adda can begin at 11 AM and somehow continue until evening.

4. The Food Culture of Sunday lunch is serious business.
Typical stars include:
Mutton Curry
Luchi
Kosha Mangsho
Mishti
For many households:
Sunday = Mangsho Day
The smell of spices cooking from morning itself announces that it is not an ordinary day.

5. Stories, Books, and Leisure
Bengali culture has a long relationship with reading.
> A Sunday afternoon often means:
> A novel by Rabindranath Tagore
> A detective story featuring Feluda
> Adventures of Professor Shonku

6. The Sacred Afternoon Nap
Known unofficially as:
"Bhater Ghum" (the sleep after lunch).
After rice, fish or mutton, and perhaps a sweet, many Bengali homes enter a state of peaceful silence.

Many Bengalis carry a strange mix of emotions on Sunday evening, and slow leisure is why Sunday occupies a special place in the Bengali imagination. It is less a calendar date and more a weekly festival of comfort. ❤️

Repost if you could relate. ♻️

text:
How to create AI ads in minutes, step by step. 🤔 


See, the goal isn't to make AI look real. 
It is to make people stop scrolling, pay attention, and take action.
Nobody buys because an ad was "100% AI-proof."



1. Conceptualisation is the MOST Important.
Before generating anything, answer:

→ Who is this ad for?
→ What action should they take?
→ What emotion should they feel?
→ Is it a static, carousel, or video ad?

Good outputs come out of clarity.



2. Write the concept.

Feed it your brief + visual concept.

Ask for:

→ A headline under 7 words
→ One line that creates curiosity or desire
→ A specific CTA



Make sure the concept is unique. For example, I imagined Mokobara  at Hogwarts.



3. Generate the creative.


Use tools like:

→ Gemini or OpenArt for Concept
→ Higgsfield
→ Kling
→ Runway


The better your prompt, the better your output.

Include:

✓ Subject or product
✓ Setting/background
✓ Mood and lighting
✓ Visual style



Example:

"A young professional enjoying coffee in a cozy café, warm morning light, shallow depth of field, minimalist aesthetic, premium lifestyle photography, product-focused composition."



4. Test before scaling.



→ Auto-resize for every platform
→ Which headline gets clicks?
→ Which visual stops the scroll?
→ Which CTA drives conversions?



The market will tell you what works.

Your job is to listen.



Sangeet Agrawal  Akarshan Gupta  Khushi Jalan

How to use Gemini Omni for AI Video Generation:

1. Go to Gemini App.
2. Create your Avatar in 2 minutes
3. Start a new chat and select your Avatar.

Gemini Omni lets you generate videos from text, images, or existing video clips.

Here's what you'll get:
→ Cinematic AI-generated videos.
→ Natural language video editing.
→ Character and scene consistency across iterations.
→ Realistic physics, lighting, and camera movements.

To create your first video:

1. Upload an image, video, or start with a text prompt.
2. Describe exactly what you want.

Example:
"Create a cinematic shot of a violinist performing in an abandoned warehouse. Warm golden lighting, dust particles floating in the air, slow camera pan from behind the musician."

3. Click Generate.

Gemini Omni will create a video based on your prompt.

Now the fun part: editing through conversation.

Instead of redoing the entire prompt, simply continue the chat:

→ "Keep everything the same, but make it rain."
→ "Change the violinist's jacket to bright red."
→ "Add dramatic lightning in the background."
→ "Make the camera slowly orbit around the subject."

Gemini remembers the context and updates the video accordingly.

You can also:
→ Turn images into animated clips.
→ Extend existing scenes.
→ Change art styles (anime, cinematic, 3D, line-art, etc.).
→ Experiment with camera angles and motion.

Once you're happy with the result:

1. Click Export.
2. Download your video.

Google automatically adds a SynthID watermark for AI transparency.

The ability to create, edit, and iterate on videos through simple conversation makes Gemini Omni one of the most powerful AI video tools available today.

text:
7,981 connection requests sitting in my inbox. 😥


I used to stress about this.

Replying to everyone. Accepting fast. Being “available”.

Then I stopped.

Because here’s what I’ve actually learned after
years of writing on LinkedIn:

	1.	“Reply to every request immediately” - No. Some sit for weeks. The right people don’t mind.

	2.	“DM everyone who wants to connect” - No. I DM the people I’m genuinely curious about. Not to sell. Just to talk.

	3.	“Grow your network aggressively” - No. I wrote. Consistently. Honestly. And 7,981 people showed up on their own.

	4.	“Always be accessible” - No. I have 380K+ Followers. I practically can’t. 

TL;DR:
	1.	Let requests wait. The right ones stay.
	2.	DM curiosity, not pipeline.
	3.	Write well. Inbound follows.
	4.	Protect your energy like it’s your job(it actually is!).

Now…
What’s a LinkedIn “best practice” you quietly stopped following?

(Would love to know 👇)

text:
At 17, I thought I'd have everything figured out by 27. 😄 

Career figured out.
Relationships settled.
A clear roadmap ahead.

Instead, it feels like standing at a crossroads with twenty different maps.

1. The Motherhood Dilemma

Lately, I’ve been thinking about motherhood. No, I am not ready.

But for the first time, it feels like a decision that exists on a timeline.

And that’s a strange thing to carry. 

2. The Growth Paradox

There’s a version of me that wants adventure.

To build.
To create.
To travel.
To become everything she’s capable of becoming.

And another version that dreams of a slower, softer life.

Both feel real. I don't know which is me?

3. The Fig Tree Analogy

The hardest part of growing up isn’t choosing what you want.

It’s realizing you can’t choose everything. Every yes quietly becomes a no to something else.

I keep thinking about the fig tree analogy.

A tree full of beautiful figs.

Each fig represents a different future.

A career.
A family.
A city.
A passion.
A dream.

And the fear isn’t choosing the wrong fig. It’s watching them all shrivel while you’re trying to choose.

4. What if I waste my potential?

What if I never become everything I could be?
Maybe that’s what turning 27 feels like.
Not fear of failure.
Fear of unrealized potential.
Fear of becoming less than who you could have been.

5. Ambition or Contentment??

Wanting more while learning to appreciate enough. 
I am so blessed with a wonderful career, friends, partner, family....and yet, why do I want more?
Should I want more? Or this is a good deal already?


I don't have answers, only questions.

Can you tell me, what you think?

text:
Did AI write this?

That's what I am thinking everytime I read an OBVIOUS AI content.

Here's how you can stay human, even if you use AI tools. 🤔 

1. Feed it your voice before you ask for anything

AI doesn't know how you talk. You have to show it.
Before writing a single post, paste in 3-5 of your best past pieces and say: "This is how I write. Match this tone exactly."

Things to remember:
a. Include posts where you were at your most natural
b. Point out specific phrases you use often
c. Tell it what you never say ("I never use corporate jargon" / "I always write short sentences")

2. Use AI for structure. Use your brain for the insight.

Here's where most people go wrong.
They ask AI for the idea AND the execution. 😒 
The result? Content that sounds like everyone else's content.

Top marketers flip this:
> They bring the original insight, the contrarian take, the lived experience.
> AI handles the skeleton, the formatting, the flow.

Your unique point of view is the only thing AI cannot replicate.
Protect it. Lead with it. Every single time.

Note:
a. Log your insights in chats, notes.
b. You can use Wispr Flow as well for this.
c. Make sure the AI Matches your intent in the output.

3. The "1st draft human, 2nd draft AI" method

Don't open AI first.
Write your messy, unfiltered first draft by hand. Even 5 bullet points. Even half a paragraph. Then hand it to AI and say: "Clean this up. Keep my voice. Don't change the ideas."

AI becomes your editor, instead of you being AI's medium!

4. Build a "voice vault" and update it monthly

Your best posts. 
Your most-used phrases. 
Your opinions on 10 key topics in your niche.
Compile all of it into one document and make it an .md file.

It's a one-time investment that pays every single time you open a prompt.
Top creators treat this like their most valuable asset.

Pro tip: 
a. Include your hot takes 
b. Add examples of sentences you'd never write alongside ones you love 
c. Refresh it every 4 weeks as your voice evolves

5. Read every AI draft out loud before posting

This is the final filter. The one most people skip.
If you stumble while reading it, rewrite that line.
If it sounds like a press release, rewrite that section.

Your audience follows YOU. Not a polished, optimized, frictionless version of you.

AI doesn't kill authentic voices.
Lazy prompting does.

Found this useful? Repost it for a fellow creator who's struggling to sound human online. ♻️

Follow me for more frameworks on AI, marketing, and building a brand that actually sounds like you.

text:
If I could DM myself at 19, here's everything I'll tell her.


- Stop waiting for permission to pitch. 🤔 

Nobody is going to tap you on the shoulder and say "you're ready now." That moment doesn't exist. The pitch IS how you get ready. Send it before you feel qualified. Send it especially before you feel qualified.

- The ₹500 project is not a stepping stone. It's a trap. You think you're building a portfolio. You're actually building a reputation for being cheap. The clients you attract at ₹500 will refer you to other ₹500 clients. Price is positioning. You chose yours.

- Stop perfecting the portfolio.

Start pitching with what you have. You spent four months redesigning your website (all equally bad!). Four months. For a website 100 people see.

- The people you're trying to impress aren't watching YOU.

They are far better than you and at a different stage of their work/career. Figure out how to make them watch your content, and they will hire you eventually.

- One skill, taken seriously, beats five skills taken casually.

You learned copywriting, then pivoted to writing, then to "content strategy," then back to marketing? Choose hard.Go embarrassingly deep. The market pays for depth.

- Pitch ten people today. Not tomorrow. Not after you redo the bio. Not after you get one more testimonial. And don't take it personally, no one owes you anything.


The gap between where I was at 19 and where I am at 26 isn't talent.
It's the number of times I sent the pitch+showed up anyway.
That's the whole thing. I wish it were more complicated.

P.S. What's the one thing your 19-year-old self needed to hear that nobody said?

text:
I used to steal my cousin brother's Maaza. 🫣

Not borrowed. Stole. Drank the whole thing. Hid the empty bottle under my bed like evidence.
He found it anyway. I got into massive trouble. . Zero regrets. 😌

That's my earliest Maaza memory, and honestly, it tells you everything about what this drink does to people. It makes you do irrational things. It makes otherwise reasonable siblings into tiny criminals.

Maaza turns 50 today.

And fifty years of making people fight over the last bottle, sneak sips when nobody's looking, and negotiate with their moms for just one more, that's not a product milestone. That's a culture one.

Behind every bottle is something bigger too: Indian summers, the farmers who grew the mangoes we grew up on, and a brand that somehow stayed exactly itself while everything around it changed.

That's rare. That's worth 50 candles.
Here's to half a century of the drink worth stealing.
Going to pour myself one right now, legally, this time.

🥭
#MaazaTurns50 #IndiaKaMango #Nostalgia #BrandHeritage #IndianSummers

text:
The hardest part about doing well in business?

Sale seasons! 🤯

As a content creator with almost 400K+ Followers, thankfully sales have never been a problem(yet).

But managing demand is. Especially during launch weeks.
It's the strangest part of running an agency. My clients are drowning in their own peak season chaos.
At this point you realise, you don't lose customers because your offer is bad. 

You lose them because:

→ Your website is so cluttered that buyers never even see the offer most relevant to them 
→ A payment fails at checkout and nobody follows up - abandoned cart, lost sale 
→ A lead says "send details" and gets a wall of text that leads to decision paralysis 
→ An unexpected error or slow load time makes your business look less credible at the worst moment 
→ You forgot FAQs, and the 2-3 questions buyers had were the exact ones that would have closed them

That part nobody talks about. As my business grew, I realised helping brands win more customers wasn't just about strategy. 
Operations matter. 
The smoother the buying experience, the more people actually convert.

Here's what that looks like in practice:

→ Separate Razorpay payment pages for different offers, each one acts like a focused single-view page instead of one long confusing flow 
→ Quick WhatsApp follow-ups with a Razorpay payment link so clients can pay without starting over 
→ Specific pitch decks on Canva ready to go if someone needs more context before deciding 
→ Loading speed checks using PageSpeed Insights before every launch 
→ FAQs written with Claude, paired with a clear refund note, removes the last bit of hesitation
The best thing I did for my revenue this sale season wasn't a new offer.

It was making the existing ones easier to say yes to.

text:
I got married last year.

I've been thinking about this a lot. Talking to friends. Reading the research. And what I found was both unsurprising and deeply uncomfortable.

Here are 15 things that change for a woman's career in India after marriage.

Some happened to me, some I watched happen to women around me:

1. People expect the woman to naturally relocate. And if she is not willing to, it’s seen as a NO-GO.
2. Your schedule is no longer just yours. You have to adjust around your new household.
3. People question the woman a lot. Why this, why that? The man? Not so much.
4. You're suddenly the default person for every ‘domestic’ decision.
5. The earnings of married women decrease by 15–20% on average. 
6. Your ambitions get reframed as "priorities" by everyone around you.
7. In-laws have opinions about your job. 
8. You're asked "so what does your husband do?" before they ask what YOU do.
9. Travel for work becomes complicated in ways it never was before.
10. You carry the mental load of the home, invisibly, constantly.
11. Your identity at work quietly competes with your new identity at home.
12. Some opportunities feel too risky now. You have more to "protect."
13. Man helping at home? AMAZING! You doing the same? Expected.
14. You're expected to want a baby soon. Whether you do or not, it follows you.
15. Your salary starts feeling like a "contribution" rather than your own.

According to research, just 31% of working women in India are married, indicating that many opt out (or are pushed out) following marriage or relocation.

I'm one of the lucky ones with support, flexibility, and work I love.

But luck shouldn't be the variable.

To every woman navigating this right now, you're not imagining it. It is harder. And it shouldn't be.

What would actually help? Workplace flexibility. Real partner support. Employers who don't quietly downgrade women post-marriage.

Let's talk about this more openly.

#WomenAtWork #GenderEquality #IndianWomen #CareerAndMarriage #WomenInLeadership

I have almost 400K+ Followers on LinkedIn.

Here's some honest truths about building a personal brand that nobody posts because it doesn't look inspiring:

• Your niche will find you. Stop trying to reverse-engineer it.
• The person with 2,000 followers making ₹5L/month exists. You just don't see them because they're not performing.
• Charging more is a marketing strategy. Price is the first thing people judge quality by.
• Most "authenticity" on LinkedIn is carefully edited authenticity. It still counts.
• The algorithm didn't shadowban you. You just posted and went offline.
• Writing "I'm open to opportunities" and doing nothing else is not a job search.
• Your first 100 posts are practice. Post them anyway.
• A good offer + a bad caption beats a bad offer + a perfect caption every time.
• People buy outcomes, not processes. Lead with what changes for them.
• If your profile gives me no reason to follow you, I won't. Fix the bio first.
• Done > Perfect. Published > Polished. Sent > Scheduled.
• The ROI on showing up consistently for a year is insane. Almost nobody does it.

text:
Mother’s Day campaigns often fall into the trap of sentimentality without behaviour. 😭

But what Bosch does interestingly in their #JustHowSheLikesIt campaign is anchoring the emotion in something deeply everyday: cooking for someone you love, and wanting to get it exactly right for them.

One of the smartest things the brand does in Masaba Gupta’s film is resist the temptation to make the Bosch Combi Steam Oven feel over-explained.

Instead, the appliance is discovered through use - through the process of cooking, reacting, adjusting, observing textures, noticing consistency and trying to recreate her mother’s famous rotizza, just how she likes it.

That changes the nature of the endorsement entirely.

Masaba isn’t “selling” the product. She’s engaging with it in a real context while doing something emotionally meaningful. And in that process, the oven’s USPs - even cooking, precision, ease and reliability - reveal themselves organically through outcomes rather than claims.

That’s what makes the advocacy feel far more credible.
The product earns relevance within the story instead of interrupting it.

Increasingly, that’s what audiences respond to: brands and products that integrate naturally into behaviour and emotion, rather than sitting outside it as obvious branding.

And Bosch understands that distinction remarkably well here. 👏

Watch the campaign film here: 
https://lnkd.in/dcNuerbw
